To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the impedance spectra of materials systems can be significantly distorted by apparatus contributions and that these artifacts can be eliminated by careful design of the experimental apparatus and application of null-correction procedures.

(1) the impedance of an electrical system is a function of the impedance of the system's components, including the sample, the leads, the sample holder, and the cabling, and (2) the impedance of the cabling is a function of its length, the number of bends, and the number of connections.

1) the impedance spectra of materials systems can be significantly altered at high frequencies by the apparatus used to measure them; 2) the effects of apparatus contributions on impedance spectra can be reduced by shielding and by null-correction procedures; and 3) the null-correction procedures are most useful at frequencies where the impedance of the apparatus is greater than the impedance of the sample.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new impedance spectrometer that is optimized for the measurement of high-frequency (100 kHz to 100 MHz) impedance spectra of materials systems.
the accurate measurement of the impedance of a material system.
the accurate measurement of impedance spectra and the correction of artifacts arising from experimental limitations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
impedance measurements are not as easy as they may appear to be.
impedance measurements of high frequency systems should be made with a guarded cell and with a high frequency impedance bridge.
impedance spectroscopy is an extremely useful tool, and that with care it can yield accurate results over a broad frequency range.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while it is not possible to remove all artifacts arising from apparatus limitations in the frequency domain, it is possible to minimize them to a level where they do not obscure the sample response.
impedance measurements are not always as simple as one would hope, and that the most careful attention to detail is required for the best results.
, in the absence of a high-frequency artifact, the accuracy of an impedance measurement is limited by the instrument and sample holder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the high-frequency response in the measured impedance spectra of samples is often not a true sample response but is an artifact of the experimental apparatus.
impedance measurements are often more complex than they seem, especially at high-frequency.
the impedance of materials systems should be determined from the data in the frequency range where the apparatus contribution is small.
